newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's Japan-contract ban widens in islands row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Japan-contract ban widens in islands row.

text.p: The Taiwan provincial assembly voted on Tuesday to exclude Japanese firms from local contracts to protest Japan's assertion of sovereignty over a chain of uninhabited East China Sea islands, an official said.
In a resolution, the Taiwan Provincial Council called for a boycott of all Japanese goods and an immediate halt to all purchasing contracts with Japan, the council official said by telephone.

Calls for boycotting Japanese goods and other anti-Japanese protests have mushroomed in recent weeks after Japanese coast guard ships repelled private Taiwan vessels nearing the Diaoyu islands, called the Senkakus in Japanese.
Taiwan's biggest county, Taipei County, voted last week to exclude Japanese firms from county construction contracts and called for a boycott of Japanese goods.
On Sunday, protesters disrupted a Japanese department store by filling shopping carts with Japan-made goods, allowing cashiers to total their prices -- then refusing to pay.
"The Japanese are invading our territory, so why are we still buying Japanese products?" one protester said.
Tuesday's resolution is binding on contracts with Taiwan's provincial government but does not affect those with the island's Republic of China central government.
Both have extensive business with Japanese contractors.
The sanctions would stand until the mounting dispute over the islands is resolved, the official said.
Popular anger simmered on Tuesday over Tokyo's claim to the tiny islands, which are northeast of Taiwan and southeast of Japan's Okinawa.
The private Association for the Protection of Diaoyu Islands launched a new round of telephone protests, bombarding Japan's two Taiwan visa offices with calls denouncing Japan's moves.
"We hope to express the voice of Taiwan's people," a member of the group said. "Japan should get out of the Diaoyu islands."

A group of paroled criminals, saying they were tired of government inaction, announced they would mount a "dare-to-die" mission in late September to bomb the lighthouse built on one of the islands by the rightist nationalist Japan Youth Federation.

The long dormant sovereignty dispute over the islands erupted in July after the lighthouse was built, angering rival claimants Taiwan and China. It intensified when Japan's coast guard ships drove off the Taiwan vessels nearing the islands.
The row has triggered anti-Japanese and increasingly nationalist protests among Chinese in Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan and mainland China.
Taiwan's central government has appealed for calm and has vowed to resolve the dispute with Japan through negotiations on fishing rights that could start in early October.

"The Japanese side should have a formal response very soon," Vice Foreign Minister Cheng Chien-jen said on state television on Tuesday. "We should be able to have a second round of dialogue in early October concerning fishing rights."
Many Taiwanese have criticised their government for taking what they see as too conciliatory a stance toward Tokyo and some have even suggested that Taipei enlist mainland China's help.
Taiwan and the mainland have been separated since the end of their civil war in 1949 when the defeated Republic of China government took refuge on Taiwan.
